name: ROI
seoDesc: ROI: work out ROI (Basic ROI) from the investment period and the rate of return. A free finance calculator with the formula, units and a worked example.
summary: ROI (Basic ROI) is what the ROI calculator works out, and it gets there from the investment period, the rate of return, the returned amount and the start date. Think of it as a shortcut for a budget, a loan conversation, a payslip check or a what-if before you talk to a lender. The unit chips sit next to the boxes, which is where most hand-calculation mistakes start.

sections.title: How does the ROI calculator work?
sections.html:
The ROI calculator takes the values in the form, applies the relationship described below and reports ROI (Basic ROI) in the results panel.

Working from the top of the form: you choose the option that describes your case (the periodic contribution (Basic ROI), the I want to find (Annualized ROI) and the periodic contribution (Second investment)); then you give the start date (Annualized ROI) and the end date (Annualized ROI of 2nd investment); then you type in the investment period, the rate of return (Basic ROI), the returned amount (Basic ROI) and the annualized ROI (Annualized ROI).

Press Calculate and the page works through the equation with the values you supplied and derives the rest; it then keeps up with you as you correct a typo.

Because the equation can be rearranged for each of its variables, the page also runs backwards. Leave the box you want to know empty, fill in the rest, and it solves for the missing one instead. That is useful when you know the answer you need rather than the inputs you have.

sections.title: The formula behind the ROI calculator
sections.html:
The page rests on a handful of relationships. Each one can be rearranged for any of its variables, which is what makes the calculator work in both directions:

ROI=(-1461 × initial invested amount − 4 × periodic contribution amount × periodic contribution × investment period + 1461 × returned amount) ÷ (1461 × initial invested amount + 4 × periodic contribution amount × periodic contribution × investment period)
Initial invested amount=(rate of return + 1 ^ -4 ÷ 1461 × investment period) × (periodic contribution amount × periodic contribution × (1 − ((periodic contribution + rate of return) ÷ periodic contribution, (4 ÷ 1461) × periodic contribution × investment period)) + rate of return × returned amount) ÷ rate of return
Initial invested amount=-gain or loss − 4 ÷ 1461 × periodic contribution amount × periodic contribution × investment period + returned amount
End date=start date + investment period
Annualized ROI=(ROI, investment period)
Time difference=(ROI, annualized ROI)

Read it as an ordinary equation. Where a word appears instead of a letter, it is the label of one of the boxes in the form; where a function appears, it is the usual mathematical meaning of that function.

If a number looks wrong, check three things in this order: that the units match what you had in mind, that no drop-down is still on its default, and that the value you entered is on the same scale as the rest — a rate typed as 5 rather than 0.05 is the classic mistake. Those three account for almost every answer that is out by a factor.

sections.title: How are units and precision handled?
sections.html:
Every quantity with units carries a chip beside its box. Switching the chip does not change what you know, only how it is written: values are converted to a common internal base, the arithmetic happens there, and the answer is converted back for display. Mixing metres with feet in one calculation is therefore safe.

Display rounding is separate from calculation rounding: the digits you see are shortened, the value behind them is not. Numbers far from everyday size are shown in scientific notation so the significant digits stay readable.

sections.title: When should you use it?
sections.html:
The ROI calculator earns its place in the middle of a task, not instead of one. It is most useful when:

  • Comparing two offers that quote their costs in different ways
  • Building a monthly budget and testing how one number shifts the rest
  • Preparing questions for a lender, an accountant or an adviser
  • Any time the same 4 figures keep coming back — the investment period, the rate of return and the returned amount — and you would rather not repeat the arithmetic by hand each time.

sections.title: How do you get a reliable answer?
sections.html:
• Change one input at a time when you are exploring. Two simultaneous changes make it impossible to tell which one moved the result.
  • Round only at the end. The calculator carries full precision internally, so re-entering a value you already rounded is the fastest way to introduce drift.
  • Write the answer down with its unit. A bare number copied into a report later is exactly where units get lost.
  • Leave the field you want solved for empty rather than guessing at it. Filling every box tells the calculator you already know the answer.

sections.title: What else is worth knowing?
sections.html:
• Filling in more than one box is fine. The most recently edited field is the one treated as known, so you can switch direction without reloading.
  • Answers that depend on a drop-down reflect the option you picked, not a range. Switching to a neighbouring option is the quickest way to see how much that factor matters.
  • Some options are backed by reference tables that ship with the page, so the values are fixed data rather than a live lookup.
  • Dates are compared date to date in your own time zone, so a daylight-saving change will not shift the count by a day.
  • Fields that are still blank are exactly the ones the calculator has not yet been given, so the results panel is a reliable map of what is missing.

faq.q: What does the ROI calculator work out?
faq.a: It returns ROI (Basic ROI), derived from the investment period, the rate of return and the returned amount. Every field in the form feeds the same relationship: press Calculate once and changing any of them updates the result immediately, with no page reload.

faq.q: What do I need to enter to use the ROI calculator?
faq.a: The form asks for the investment period, the rate of return, the returned amount and the start date, which is 17 fields in total. Each one is labelled with what it means and, where relevant, the unit it expects. Anything you leave blank is treated as the value to solve for.

faq.q: Can I enter investment period in a different unit?
faq.a: Yes. Investment period opens in years and the chip beside it offers 27 units. The number you typed keeps its magnitude and only its label changes; the calculation itself happens in a common base unit, so mixing systems in one form is safe.
Yes. Each variable in the relationship can be the one being solved for: fill in the answer you are aiming at, leave the field you want empty, and the calculator inverts the equation for you.

faq.q: How much do the drop-down choices change the answer?
faq.a: There are several choices to make (6 in total), and each one selects a different case rather than scaling the result. Switching a single option and watching the result is the fastest way to see how much that choice is worth.

With the values the page starts from, the calculator reports Periodic contribution amount = 0. Treat that as a reference point rather than a recommendation: it exists so you can tell at a glance whether your own inputs are on the same scale.

faq.q: Is the ROI calculator free to use?
faq.a: Yes — no account, no sign-up and no limit on how many times you run it. The arithmetic happens in your browser, so the values you type are not sent anywhere.
